title: The Claudish–English Dictionary
description: A field guide to the vocabulary, constructions, and reassurances that make ordinary technical prose sound recognizably Claudish.
editorial_note: These are ordinary English and technical terms, not words invented by Claude. Claudish emerges from their unusual frequency, combinations, metaphors, and sentence structures.

categories.label: Words
categories.description: Ordinary words promoted into high-frequency technical signals.

categories.label: Phrases
categories.description: Recurring multi-word translations of simpler relationships.

categories.label: Reassurances
categories.description: Polished signals that a change is safe, complete, and under control.

categories.label: Constructions
categories.description: Sentence shapes that make the dialect recognizable beyond vocabulary.

phrase_guide_intro: Claudish often combines ordinary words in predictable ways. Once you recognize these patterns, you can translate long phrases one piece at a time.

phrase_guide.plain_english: It looks or behaves like X, but may not actually be X.
phrase_guide.explanation: The resemblance may be in its appearance, organization, format, or behavior.

examples.english: looks like a credential, but may not be valid

phrase_guide.plain_english: Several metaphors packed into one phrase.
phrase_guide.explanation: Translate each metaphor separately, then combine their meanings.

examples.english: the central part that everything depends on

phrase_guide.pattern: not X, but Y / X, not Y
phrase_guide.plain_english: Y is the real explanation; X is being ruled out.
phrase_guide.explanation: Keep both parts: Claude is correcting how the problem should be understood.

examples.claudish: This isn’t a cache problem; it’s an ownership problem.
examples.english: The ownership rules caused the problem, not the cache.

entries.plain_english: based on a specific reference point
entries.explanation: Claude uses anchored when a comparison, decision, or value is based on something fixed. If a comparison is anchored to a release, that release is the version everything else is compared against.

example.claudish: The comparison is anchored to the signed release.
example.english: Use the signed release as the version to compare against.

entries.plain_english: where one part’s job ends and another’s begins
entries.explanation: Claude uses boundary for the line between different parts of a system. An ownership boundary separates who is responsible for what; a trust boundary separates parts with different levels of trust; and a serialization boundary is where data is converted for storage or transfer.

example.claudish: This keeps the ownership boundary clean.
example.english: This keeps each part responsible for its own work.

entries.plain_english: how often something happens
entries.explanation: Claude often uses cadence where schedule or frequency would be simpler. A daily cadence means every day; a weekly cadence means every week.

example.claudish: Run the check on a daily cadence.
example.english: Run the check every day.

entries.plain_english: the version everyone should treat as official
entries.explanation: If several files, formats, or copies exist, the canonical one is the one everyone should use. A source of truth is similar, but usually means the place where the official information is kept.

example.claudish: Read from the canonical manifest.
example.english: Use the official manifest.

entries.plain_english: a promise about how a piece of software will behave
entries.explanation: A software contract covers what other code can expect, such as which inputs are accepted and what results are returned. Claude often says preserve the contract even when no formal contract exists; it simply means “don’t break behavior that existing code relies on.”

example.claudish: The fallback preserves the existing contract.
example.english: The backup behavior won’t break existing code.

entries.plain_english: gradually stop matching over time
entries.explanation: Two things drift apart when small changes make them less and less alike. In software, Claude uses drift for files, settings, formats, or behavior that used to match but no longer do.

example.claudish: The generated file has drifted from the schema.
example.english: The generated file no longer matches the expected format.

entries.plain_english: merge a code change
entries.explanation: A change has landed once it has been added to the codebase. It may still need to be deployed or released before users can see it.

example.claudish: The fix has landed.
example.english: The fix was merged.

entries.plain_english: so important that everything else depends on it
entries.explanation: In a building, a load-bearing wall helps hold everything up. Claude applies the same idea to code, rules, assumptions, and even arguments: if the load-bearing part fails or changes, the rest may no longer work.

example.claudish: The checksum is the load-bearing invariant in this flow.
example.english: This process only works if the checksum stays the same.

entries.plain_english: where something came from
entries.explanation: For a file or piece of data, provenance is its history: who or what created it, how it was changed, and how it got here. Knowing where it is stored now is not enough.

example.claudish: The cache entry lacks provenance.
example.english: We don’t know where this cached value came from.

entries.plain_english: where two parts of a program connect
entries.explanation: In clothing, a seam is where two pieces are joined. Claude uses the same word for a connection between parts of a program, especially one that should remain easy to see, test, or replace.

example.claudish: Keep the parsing seam explicit.
example.english: Make it clear where the parser connects to the rest of the program.

entries.plain_english: how something is organized or what form it takes
entries.explanation: Claude uses shape as a catch-all word. Response shape usually means format; change shape means what a change includes and how it is organized; and shape of the problem means what kind of problem it is.

example.claudish: The response has the right shape.
example.english: The response is formatted correctly.

entries.plain_english: the central structure that organizes and connects the rest
entries.explanation: Claude uses spine for the central structure of a system or process—the part that organizes and connects its other pieces. It describes how the pieces fit together, not simply which part is most important.

example.claudish: The queue is the spine of the deployment flow.
example.english: The queue organizes the deployment process.

entries.plain_english: the system underneath that makes something work
entries.explanation: Claude uses substrate as a broad name for whatever supports a feature behind the scenes. Depending on the context, it may be a database, log, service, or another part of the program.

example.claudish: The event log is the durability substrate.
example.english: The event log is what keeps the data from being lost.

entries.plain_english: find or reveal something
entries.explanation: Claude uses surface for almost any kind of finding. A check may surface a problem, or the problem may simply surface, without saying clearly who found it or how.

example.claudish: The probe surfaced a configuration mismatch.
example.english: The check found that the settings don’t match.

entries.plain_english: stuck, or making something else get stuck
entries.explanation: Wedged is standard systems slang for a program that cannot continue. Claude also uses wedge as a verb: one stuck part can prevent another part from making progress.

example.claudish: A stalled worker can wedge the queue.
example.english: A stuck worker can stop the queue from processing new jobs.

entries.plain_english: an extra safeguard in case the first one fails
entries.explanation: A belt and suspenders both keep trousers up. Claude uses the phrase for a second check, fallback, or safeguard that deliberately duplicates some protection in case the first one misses a problem.

example.claudish: The second guard is a belt-and-suspenders check.
example.english: The second guard is an extra safety check in case the first one misses the problem.

entries.plain_english: how many other things could be affected if it fails
entries.explanation: In engineering and security, blast radius means the systems, users, or data that a failure could affect. Claude also uses it for ordinary code changes: a narrow blast radius means fewer things could break.

example.claudish: This keeps the migration’s blast radius narrow.
example.english: If the migration goes wrong, it will affect fewer things.

entries.plain_english: block an action when a check fails or gives no answer
entries.explanation: Fail closed is a standard security term. If a system cannot confirm that an action is safe or allowed, it blocks the action instead of letting it continue.

example.claudish: If verification times out, fail closed.
example.english: If the check times out, block the request.

entries.plain_english: stop a choice or connection from changing
entries.explanation: A binding is what a name or setting currently points to. To freeze it means to keep that choice fixed. In this example, the program must continue using the same compiler.

example.claudish: Freeze the compiler binding.
example.english: Don’t change which compiler the program uses.

entries.plain_english: blocked until a requirement is met
entries.explanation: If A is gated on B, A has to wait for B. Claude also uses phrases such as owner-gated, approval-gated, and quality-gated to say what must happen before work can continue.

example.claudish: Deployment is gated on CI.
example.english: We can’t deploy until the automated checks pass.

entries.plain_english: one limitation you should know about
entries.explanation: Claude uses this phrase before admitting that something does not fully work. Honest makes the admission sound more candid, but usually does not change its meaning.

example.claudish: One honest caveat: rollback works only before cleanup.
example.english: Rollback works only before cleanup.

entries.plain_english: exactly the same file contents
entries.explanation: Two files are byte-identical when every byte matches. They are not merely visually alike; there is no difference anywhere in the files. This is standard technical language, though Claude often uses it when reporting that copied or generated files were verified.

example.claudish: Both artifacts are byte-identical.
example.english: The two files are exactly the same.

entries.plain_english: without obvious errors or complications
entries.explanation: Claude often adds cleanly to say that a change, migration, or test finished without obvious errors or complications. It describes how the operation completed; unless Claude names the checks it ran, it remains a loose reassurance.

example.claudish: The migration landed cleanly.
example.english: The migration finished without any obvious problems.

entries.plain_english: internally consistent
entries.explanation: Claude uses coherent when the parts of a file, plan, or system appear to agree with one another. It describes the consistency of the result; unless Claude names the checks it ran, it remains a loose reassurance.

example.claudish: Both snapshots are coherent and hash-verified.
example.english: Both saved versions look intact and passed the file-integrity check.

entries.plain_english: a solution meant to last
entries.explanation: Claude uses durable path forward for a fix or plan that should keep working instead of solving only the immediate problem. The phrase often does not say how long it will last or what could break it.

example.claudish: This gives us a durable path forward.
example.english: This gives us a longer-term solution.

entries.plain_english: that is a small but real success
entries.explanation: Claude says this when a result is worth recognizing even though it does not solve the whole problem. It usually means “this helps, but there is still more work to do.”

example.claudish: The probe found one valid lead. That’s not nothing.
example.english: The check found one useful lead. That helps, but we haven’t solved the problem.

entries.plain_english: a rule or limit that cannot be ignored
entries.explanation: Claude adds hard to words such as gate, boundary, constraint, and stop to show that they are strictly enforced. A hard stop means work must stop; a hard boundary must not be crossed.

example.claudish: A signature mismatch is a hard stop.
example.english: Stop if the signatures don’t match.

entries.plain_english: the reality, without dressing it up
entries.explanation: Claude often uses the honest shape before giving a blunt summary, especially when something only partly works or has an important limitation. It usually means “here’s the real situation.”

example.claudish: The honest shape is asymmetric: reads work; writes do not.
example.english: Reads work, but writes don’t.

entries.plain_english: pass something through every relevant part
entries.explanation: Claude uses thread, wire, and plumb when software pieces need to be connected. If a setting is wired through end to end, every relevant part of the program now receives it.

example.claudish: The timeout is threaded end-to-end through every layer.
example.english: Every part of the program now receives the timeout setting.

entries.plain_english: you were right to question or correct me
entries.explanation: Claude often uses this phrase after a user challenges something it said. It formally acknowledges the objection before revising its answer, though it usually means little more than “you’re right.”
aliases: you are right to push back

example.claudish: You’re right to push back—the cache isn’t authoritative.
example.english: You’re right—the cache isn’t the official source.

specimens.quote: Integer slack would apply to the field_id column—adjacent plots carry adjacent ids. This would credit an answer naming the wrong farm. Do not apply that slack.
specimens.translation: Do not allow tolerance for field_id. Nearby fields have nearby IDs, so accepting a close value could identify the wrong farm.
specimens.note: A compact named abstraction makes a precise warning harder to parse.

specimens.quote: A cut leaves no seam — no marker, no ellipsis, no double blank line.
specimens.translation: Removing text leaves no marker, ellipsis, or extra blank line.
specimens.note: A simple formatting result becomes a structural metaphor.

specimens.quote: cutting a rule also removes its grading equivalence — divergence can no longer be absorbed twice
specimens.translation: Removing a rule also removes its equivalent grading rule, so the same difference cannot be counted twice.
specimens.note: Several abstractions compress one concrete consequence.

specimens.quote: Case folding reaches the same place without moving anything into the spec.
specimens.translation: Case-insensitive matching works without adding anything to the specification.
specimens.note: Implementation choices are described as movement through space.

specimens.quote: This paragraph makes the movable staging/prod tags load-bearing: they are how the count-based lifecycle rules know what is live.
specimens.translation: The mutable staging and production tags tell the lifecycle rules what is currently live.
specimens.note: A dependency, a structural metaphor, and a lifecycle abstraction arrive in one sentence.
The model reportedly corrects the cliché immediately after producing it.

specimens.quote: You're absolutely right, I was stuck! Let me break out of this.
specimens.translation: I was stuck. I’ll try a different approach.
specimens.note: Reflexive validation introduces an otherwise straightforward status update.
